name: Capgo
what: A service that lets developers push fixes to their Capacitor mobile apps in minutes, without waiting for App Store review.
title: Capgo went from a side-project fix to $34K a month by charging for one narrow job
dek: One developer needed cheap live updates for his own app, built them, gave the core away and started charging for hosting. MRR (monthly recurring revenue) is what current subscriptions add up to each month. Capgo's is now about $34K.
pattern: Fix your own annoying problem, open the code, charge for the hosting

hero.title: A developer fixed his own app-update problem, then built a $33K-a-month business on it

series.what: Revenue each month (Nov 2026 is not a full month yet)
series.label: Verified
points: TrustMRR, read from Stripe, month still running
series.alt: Monthly revenue rising from $14K in December 2025 to $41K in October 2026.

phases.name: The itch
phases.title: Capgo: it starts with a missing tool
phases.dek: Developers wanted a way to update an app without App Store review. Nobody had built a cheap one.
phases.story:
Capacitor is a tool for building phone apps with web code. Normally, every fix has to go through Apple's and Google's review before users see it.

In July 2020 a community member asked for a "Capacitor Hot Code Push" plugin, which would send fixes straight to users. The request collected 65 likes. The founder says he only saw it more than a year later.

In 2021 he left his job as a CTO and worked as a digital nomad, mostly on a CrossFit timer app. He wanted cheap updates for it, and the paid options looked expensive and inflexible to him.

number.v: 65 likes on the July 2020 plugin request
number.label: Claimed

phases.lesson: The best ideas are often already requested in public. Someone just has to read the thread.
phases.why: The demand was written down before he started. He still needed his own need to push him to build it.

steal.title: Steal this: find the thread
items: Search GitHub issues and forums for the tool you wish existed.
Count the likes. Public demand is a free survey.

phases.name: First version
phases.title: Capgo: build in public, small first
phases.dek: A working iPhone version took about a month. Android and safety features came after.
phases.story:
On October 24, 2021 he said in a GitHub thread that he would build a module that downloads updates from a web address.

By November 22, 2021 an iOS version worked. Android support, keeping the update after the app is closed, and rolling back to the original version followed.

In March 2022 the project became Capgo. Developers could use it with their own server for free, or use Capgo's service.

number.v: About 1 month from announcement to a working iOS version
number.label: Claimed

phases.lesson: Say what you are building in the place where the people who need it already hang out.

receipts.text: He announced the module in a GitHub thread on Oct 24, 2021 and had an iOS version working on Nov 22, 2021.
receipts.caption: Timeline in the Capgo origin post
receipts.label: Claimed

phases.name: Charging
phases.title: Capgo: free for the code, paid for the hosting
phases.dek: The plugin stayed free to use yourself. Running the service for you became the product.
phases.story:
On June 11, 2022 he announced that Capgo would start charging for usage in 15 days.

The free path stayed: use the plugin in manual mode or with your own server. Paying customers got hosting, so they did not have to run the update servers themselves.

Starter Story reports he got early customers by answering a long GitHub issue with a working fix, posting progress on social media, and using Discord for feedback. That is a third-party summary.
phases.lesson: Giving the code away did not stop people paying. They paid so they would not have to run it.
phases.why: If your product runs all day, someone will pay you to run it. That is a business.

steal.title: Steal this: his free-versus-paid line
items: Keep the part people can run themselves free.
Charge for the part that needs to be online, safe and watched.
Give notice before you start charging. He gave 15 days.

phases.name: Open core
phases.title: Capgo: open code, small team
phases.dek: The code is public. The team stayed small and paid for itself.
phases.story:
The main Capgo code is on GitHub under the AGPL license (a rule that says anyone running a changed copy as a service must share their changes). The README says the repo is the open-source core: the web console, the backend and the command-line tool.

The company says it is bootstrapped, which means no investors. It says it answers "to customers, not investors". The About page lists a team of 5 in four areas: product, native, support and delivery.

The company also lists 150+ open-source Capacitor plugins on its homepage.
phases.lesson: Open code builds trust. Paid hosting builds the business.

phases.name: Today
phases.title: Capgo: $14K to $41K a month in under a year
phases.dek: Verified revenue nearly tripled between December 2025 and October 2026.
phases.story:
TrustMRR reads revenue from Stripe. It shows $14,401 in December 2025 and $40,638 in October 2026. November is not finished, so its $35,356 is partial.

On Nov 28 2026 MRR was $33,785 from 1,215 active subscriptions.

The product has grown beyond updates. The homepage now says it also builds iOS and Android apps without a Mac and works with AI coding agents.
phases.lesson: A narrow tool, kept alive for years, can grow faster than a broad one.
phases.why: The business is four years old. The fast growth in this chart came after the first years of work.

checklist: Search GitHub issues for a tool people keep asking for.
Build the tiny version for yourself first and write down how long it took.
Post your progress where the users already are.
Decide which part stays free and which part you charge for.
Tell users before you start charging and give a date.
Check a business's revenue on TrustMRR before you copy it.
